paragraphs: This paper modifies back-propagation so that learning also controls how a network uses its hidden units. The modification reduces an energy term defined from the squares of hidden-unit activations. This gives training an additional objective concerned with the internal representation, allowing the learning process to help determine how much hidden structure a task needs.

For known Boolean functions, the algorithm can find architectures described as optimal or nearly optimal. It also makes the activity of the remaining hidden units easier to interpret. These are related benefits: choosing an appropriate internal architecture can help reveal how the network represents a solution. The method also estimates suitable architectural complexity for phonetic labeling.

The authors describe adaptations of the same principle beyond architecture selection. One addresses a particular local minimum associated with a logistic activation function ranging from minus one to plus one. The abstract reports that this adaptation preserves faster convergence while encouraging binary hidden-unit activations, showing how activation-based objectives can shape both learning dynamics and representations.
neurips-1988-a-back-propagation-algorith.tldr: A modified back-propagation objective helps networks choose suitable hidden-unit architectures and develop more interpretable internal representations.

paragraphs: The Parsing and Learning System, or PALS, combines sentence parsing with learning from examples. Its task is to recover sentence structure under a context-free grammar. The system is described as massively parallel, placing parallel computation at the center of an approach to handling grammatical structure.

A central design choice is the way PALS represents parse trees: the structured descriptions produced when a sentence is parsed. The abstract attributes its ability to handle sentences of unbounded length mainly to this representation. The significance is that the representation does not impose a fixed sentence-length ceiling. This is a claim about the system's representational capability, rather than a claim that sentences of every length require the same computational effort.

PALS can also improve its parsing performance when shown training examples. This makes learning part of the parser itself, connecting the structural representation with a mechanism for improvement through experience. The contribution brings together parallel parsing, a representation that accommodates unrestricted sentence length, and adaptation driven by examples.
neurips-1988-a-massively-parallel-self-t.tldr: PALS combines massively parallel parsing with a parse-tree representation that supports unbounded sentence length and learning from examples.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a way to decide what an unsupervised feedforward network should learn: its outputs should preserve the information needed to reconstruct its inputs as well as possible. This turns reconstruction into a training objective. A useful output representation is therefore one from which the original data can be recovered effectively.

This principle gives learning a target without requiring externally supplied category labels. The input data themselves provide the reference against which the representation is judged. The authors describe a training algorithm for linear networks and for nonlinear networks with certain types of nonlinearity. That qualification matters because the stated algorithm does not cover every possible nonlinear network.

Applications are presented in image coding, feature detection, and the analysis of random-dot stereograms. These examples connect the reconstruction principle to several visual processing tasks. The shared idea is that preserving recoverable information can guide the formation of useful outputs, providing one objective that can organize learning across different applications.
neurips-1988-an-optimality-principle-for.tldr: The paper trains unsupervised networks to produce representations that preserve the ability to reconstruct their inputs.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a compact hardware implementation of a class of shunting recurrent neural networks. The implementation is entirely analog and fully parallel, and is intended to work across a range of field-effect-transistor integration technologies. The contribution connects the behavior of a recurrent network with a practical form of electronic implementation.

The network supports contrast enhancement, data compression, and adaptation to average input intensity. These capabilities make it suitable for processing sensory information, where useful features must be extracted from signals whose overall intensity can vary. The authors also identify feature extraction for content-addressable memory as an application, placing the circuit before a memory system that retrieves information by content.

The network can additionally serve as the memory itself. It has a global Lyapunov function, a mathematical property used here to support stable content-addressable storage. The proposed circuit therefore has roles in both preparing information and storing it stably. It can also operate as a front end for an analog adaptive resonance circuit.
neurips-1988-analog-implementation-of-sh.tldr: A compact analog recurrent-network design combines sensory preprocessing capabilities with mathematically supported stable associative storage.

paragraphs: The paper examines the dynamics of the Distributed Connectionist Production System, or DCPS. Its central concern is how this neural network behaves as its internal state changes. The abstract describes those dynamics as complex, motivating a way to understand the behavior of component modules more intuitively.

The authors use visualizations of the modules' energy landscapes. Such a view organizes possible network states according to an energy description, helping make the relationship between state and dynamics easier to reason about. The analysis focuses on some component modules, giving a way to inspect parts of the system rather than treating its behavior as an undifferentiated whole.

The visualizations also suggest ways to control the dynamics when the system encounters difficult cases. Their value is therefore both explanatory and practical: understanding how a module behaves can inform changes intended to improve performance. The stated contribution is an intuitive analysis that points toward control strategies; the abstract presents these strategies as suggestions arising from the landscape view.
neurips-1988-analyzing-the-energy-landsc.tldr: Visualizing energy landscapes of DCPS modules helps explain their dynamics and suggests ways to improve behavior on difficult cases.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a training method for situations in which an expert chooses among several alternatives. Each training input contains two alternatives, and the target output says which one the expert prefers. The network learns through comparisons, using the expert's relative judgments as its teaching signal.

The authors apply this approach to backgammon, where a player must select a move from the available legal moves. Comparing alternatives makes the learning task closely match the decision being demonstrated: determining which option is better. It also provides a way to learn preferences without requiring the expert to supply an absolute numerical value for each option.

The abstract reports much higher performance with smaller networks and simpler, more understandable coding schemes. It also states that the network can be arranged to always produce consistent rankings. This matters because individual pairwise judgments need to fit together when choosing from a larger set. The contribution therefore concerns both learning expert preferences efficiently and organizing those preferences into coherent orderings.
neurips-1988-connectionist-learning-of-e.tldr: Training on expert comparisons improves backgammon move selection while enabling smaller networks, simpler representations, and consistent rankings.

paragraphs: This paper studies the Boltzmann machine as a memory that retrieves stored patterns from noisy inputs. The challenge is to obtain an unambiguous stored answer while avoiding spurious states that do not represent valid memories. The authors use the machine's ability to escape local minima as part of the retrieval process.

An association rule assigns a sphere of influence to each stored pattern. Together with the network dynamics, this rule determines when a noisy input has been associated with a valid memory. Spurious fixed points outside recognized regions are skipped because the machine has a nonzero probability of escaping any state. The proposed retrieval operates at a constant temperature.

The paper provides best-case and worst-case performance bounds, with results applying to the Boltzmann machine and the asynchronous binary-threshold Hopfield model. It also enables polynomial-time studies of tradeoffs among design parameters. The significance is that retrieval behavior becomes something a designer can bound and analyze, while random state changes help prevent invalid attractors from becoming final answers.
neurips-1988-convergence-and-pattern-sta.tldr: An association rule and stochastic network dynamics enable noisy pattern retrieval that bypasses spurious states, with explicit performance bounds.

paragraphs: The paper presents a digital implementation of two-dimensional self-organizing feature maps. Its method uses subspace classification through an n-tuple technique, organizing classification around selected groups of input components. The focus is on realizing the map computationally, connecting a neural representation with operations suitable for a conventional microcomputer.

The authors also discuss approximating weight vectors and using orthogonal projections to produce a winner-take-all network. These mechanisms address how information is represented and how one response is selected from competing responses. Together, they form part of the implementation approach for turning a feature-map model into a workable digital system.

The reported implementation can apply more than one million effective binary weights in 25 milliseconds on a conventional microcomputer. This figure describes the computational capacity of the implementation, rather than a recognition accuracy. The paper also describes image recognition tasks, including character recognition and object centering. These applications connect the implementation techniques to concrete uses involving both image identity and position.
neurips-1988-digital-realisation-of-self.tldr: A digital self-organizing-map implementation applies over one million effective binary weights in 25 milliseconds and supports image recognition tasks.

paragraphs: MURPHY is a neural controller and path planner implemented with a video camera and a Rhino XR-series robot arm. Its internal representation uses four populations of simple units to describe static and changing aspects of the sensory and motor environment. This organization is inspired by the arrangement of sensory and motor maps in cerebral cortex.

Earlier work taught MURPHY a direct kinematic model through extended practice: a model of how its camera-arm system behaves. It then used that model to guide reaching toward unobstructed visual targets through heuristic search. The present work adds learning of inverse differential kinematics, allowing the controller to turn a desired direction of hand movement into corresponding arm changes.

This extension lets MURPHY move its hand directly toward a visible target without searching for that movement. A second extension addresses reaching when obstacles are present. The two developments expand different aspects of the controller: one provides a more direct route from visual goals to movement, while the other extends planning to environments where the route itself matters.
neurips-1988-further-explorations-in-vis.tldr: MURPHY adds learned inverse differential kinematics for direct visually guided movement and extends reaching to environments with obstacles.

paragraphs: GEMINI addresses a tradeoff between learning efficiency and hardware simplicity. Learning from correlations between random activity changes and reinforcement is straightforward to implement but inefficient. Back-propagation obtains more useful error information efficiently, while requiring more complex hardware. The proposed method combines aspects of these approaches for multilayer networks.

GEMINI injects noise only into the first hidden layer and observes how the output error changes. Each hidden layer has an associated linear network that iteratively inverts a matrix relating the noise to the error change. This process produces error derivatives, supplying information about how activity changes affect the error without propagating derivatives backward through the main network.

Because the method avoids back-propagation, it permits unknown nonlinearities within the system. This connects its learning mechanism to the implementation problem that motivates the paper. The abstract reports greater efficiency than correlational reinforcement procedures while retaining many of their implementation advantages. Two simulations demonstrate the method's effectiveness, supporting the proposed combination of perturbation-based measurement and matrix-based derivative estimation.
neurips-1988-gemini-gradient-estimation-.tldr: GEMINI estimates error derivatives through injected noise and iterative matrix inversion, enabling learning without back-propagation through unknown nonlinearities.

paragraphs: The paper investigates a simple recurrent network that predicts the next item in a sequence. At each step, it combines the current item with the hidden-unit activity retained from the preceding step. That recurrent connection gives past inputs a way to influence predictions through a changing internal representation.

When trained on strings generated by a particular finite-state grammar, the network can become a perfect recognizer for that grammar. The result shows that a next-item prediction task can lead the network to capture the grammar's sequential structure. The stated success concerns the particular grammar studied, rather than every possible sequence-generating system.

Cluster analyses reveal that hidden activity encodes prediction-relevant information about the entire path through the sequence. Analyses at different training stages also illustrate how this organization develops during learning. The important idea is that earlier experience can remain relevant through recurrent hidden states, without explicitly representing each previous event separately. The architecture thus connects a learning procedure local in time with representations that carry information across time.
neurips-1988-learning-sequential-structu.tldr: A simple recurrent network learns a finite-state grammar while its hidden activity retains prediction-relevant information about sequence history.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes a mathematical model of how ocular dominance columns form in mammalian visual cortex. These columns organize cells according to their preference for input from one eye. The model provides a shared framework for studying several biological mechanisms in which patterns of neural activity influence development.

The results identify conditions under which monocular cells form robustly and cortical interactions organize them into columns. In the reported sufficient conditions, inputs belonging to the same eye have locally correlated firing and are not anticorrelated within an arbor radius. Broader correlations within an eye, or anticorrelations between the eyes, make the resulting cortex more exclusively responsive to individual eyes.

Positive correlation across an arbor radius produces an almost completely monocular cortex in the model. The authors combine computational results with eigenfunction decomposition and linear stability analysis to explain most of its features. This analytical understanding allows column widths and other properties to be predicted from measurable biological parameters, linking assumptions about activity patterns to the spatial organization that develops.
neurips-1988-models-of-ocular-dominance-.tldr: A mathematical model links correlations in eye-specific neural activity to ocular dominance column formation and predicts column properties from biological parameters.

paragraphs: NADEL is a two-level neural network for early visual processing. Its lower level receives visual features on a two-dimensional map and spreads their activity over progressively larger spatial scales as time passes. This diffusion makes elapsed time part of how the network organizes visual information.

The upper level periodically receives the diffusion map's activity and uses local comparisons to find activity peaks. These peaks provide the network's output and are also fed back through connections that enhance the center and suppress the surrounding region. The interaction between spreading activity and selective enhancement produces feature clusters at multiple scales.

The authors describe uses ranging from finding corners, sharp bends, and line endings to filling contour gaps and choosing fixation points. They also identify multiscale perceptual grouping, long-range apparent-motion correspondence, and two-dimensional shape representation as applications. The common mechanism is the changing organization of local features over space and time. The proposed shape representations can tolerate changes in position, orientation, scale, and small deformations.
neurips-1988-neural-analog-diffusion-enh.tldr: NADEL combines spatial diffusion with feedback from local activity peaks to group visual features across scales over time.

paragraphs: The paper develops a self-organizing Hopfield-type network for television image compression using vector quantization. In this setting, a codebook supplies representative patterns for encoding image information. The proposed approach makes the organization of the neural network part of how an image-specific codebook is generated.

A distinctive feature is the use of metastable network states as an additional storage resource. These states offer further representational possibilities within the spin-glass-like network. The method therefore connects the collection of states available to the network with the collection of representatives available for compression.

The authors use the Minimal Overlap learning rule to optimize the organization of attractors, the states toward which the network's dynamics tend. Their self-organizing scheme produces an adaptive codebook for a given television image. The contribution lies in linking attractor organization, extra storage through metastable states, and codebook adaptation within one approach. This makes the network's internal dynamics directly relevant to the representation used for image compression.
neurips-1988-neural-approach-for-tv-imag.tldr: A self-organizing Hopfield network uses metastable states and organized attractors to generate adaptive codebooks for television image compression.

paragraphs: This paper studies neural receivers for spread-spectrum communication with multiple users. A conventional matched-filter receiver can perform poorly when interfering signals become much stronger than the desired signal, a difficulty called the near-far problem. An optimal receiver addresses this problem but is too computationally complex for practical use in the setting described.

The authors investigate multilayer perceptrons as a simpler, robust alternative. They train the networks using back-propagation and a modified version of it. The optimal receiver serves as a performance benchmark and helps identify the networks' decision regions: the portions of input space assigned to different received-signal decisions.

The study also introduces importance sampling to reduce the number of simulations needed for performance evaluation. Across every example considered, the neural receiver significantly outperforms the conventional receiver. This supports neural classification as a practical approach to interference-sensitive demodulation within the studied cases. The result establishes an advantage over the conventional method without asserting that the neural receiver equals the optimal receiver.
neurips-1988-neural-net-receivers-in-mul.tldr: Multilayer neural receivers outperform conventional matched-filter receivers in the studied multiuser spread-spectrum examples.

paragraphs: The paper describes a system for recognizing hand-printed digits using classical recognition techniques together with neural-network methods. Its training and testing data come from ZIP codes on actual U.S. mail. This grounds the task in handwriting encountered in a real application, connecting the system design to practical recognition needs.

The recognizer can reject examples that it treats as unclassifiable. It rejects a small portion of the data and achieves a very low error rate on the examples it accepts. These two outcomes belong together: the reported accuracy concerns the retained examples, while rejection allows the system to leave some inputs unresolved.

The authors report favorable comparisons with other leading recognizers. Their contribution is the combined recognition system, including its ability to distinguish accepted classifications from rejected cases. They also suggest that many of the techniques could apply to other recognition tasks, while acknowledging that some methods are specific to handwritten digits. That broader usefulness is presented as a prospect for transfer beyond the demonstrated application.
neurips-1988-neural-network-recognizer-f.tldr: A hybrid recognizer achieves very low error on accepted handwritten ZIP-code digits while rejecting a small share of difficult examples.

paragraphs: The paper discusses neural-network applications to recognizing star patterns for spacecraft attitude determination. Here, attitude means the spacecraft's orientation. Star-pattern recognition is treated as a component of determining that orientation, connecting a pattern-recognition problem with the broader task of spacecraft control.

The motivation is a mismatch between the computation needed and the onboard hardware described. Conventional serial microprocessors must handle problems that are inherently parallel, creating computational bottlenecks. The abstract places this issue in a setting where the most complex attitude determination and control tasks remain governed by ground-based systems and personnel.

Brain-inspired computing architectures are considered because they promise fast, fault-tolerant processing. Their potential value comes from matching parallel computation to the structure of the task. The paper's contribution, as stated, is a discussion of neural-network applications to star recognition within this engineering context. Speed and fault tolerance are presented as motivations and promises of the approach, rather than measured achievements reported in the abstract.
neurips-1988-neural-network-star-pattern.tldr: The paper explores neural star-pattern recognition as a response to onboard computational bottlenecks in spacecraft orientation determination.

paragraphs: This paper develops an optimization approach to vision problems that involve several levels of abstraction. Its objective functions include both compositional hierarchies, concerning how parts form larger structures, and specialization hierarchies, concerning more general and more specific descriptions. These relationships become part of what the system evaluates when interpreting visual information.

The authors express the vision tasks as inexact graph matching. A graph represents elements and relationships, while inexact matching allows correspondences that are not perfectly identical. They then formulate the matching problem as constrained optimization, giving the system an objective to improve together with conditions that acceptable matches must satisfy.

Analog neural networks perform the resulting optimization. This connects a structural description of a vision problem to a neural computation for finding a match. The framework applies to perceptual grouping and model matching, bringing both under the same formulation. The paper presents preliminary experimental results, so the stated empirical contribution is an initial demonstration of the approach.
neurips-1988-neural-networks-for-model-m.tldr: The paper formulates hierarchical visual grouping and model matching as constrained graph-matching problems solved by analog neural networks.

paragraphs: The paper concerns the barn owl's ability to orient its head toward visual or auditory stimuli. Its biological focus is a set of spatial representations in the midbrain that combine vision, hearing, and motor information. These representations connect where a stimulus is located with the head movement used to bring it into view.

The described behavior centers a stimulus within the visual field. Both a visible target and an audible target can guide this orienting response. The relevance of the fused maps is therefore their connection between sensory location and motor action: information from different senses participates in directing the same kind of movement.

The authors present models and computer simulations of these midbrain structures. This puts the relationship among visual, auditory, and motor representations into a computational setting. The supplied abstract ends before specifying the particular problems addressed or the simulation outcomes. Its supported contribution is thus the modeling of integrated spatial maps for head orientation, with the behavioral purpose of those maps clearly identified.
neurips-1988-neuronal-maps-for-sensory-m.tldr: The paper models integrated visual, auditory, and motor maps involved in directing a barn owl's head toward stimuli.

paragraphs: The paper develops mean field annealing as an alternative formulation of simulated annealing for combinatorial optimization. Stochastic annealing uses random state changes and a gradually reduced temperature to search an objective with multiple minima. The proposed method replaces discrete variables with average values computed through a mean field approximation.

The reported benefit is that equilibrium at a fixed temperature is reached one to two orders of magnitude faster than with simulated annealing. This speed claim concerns the relaxation step at a given temperature. The paper derives a general algorithmic framework and explains its relationship to Hopfield networks, connecting the optimization procedure with neural-network dynamics.

The authors study graph bipartitioning both analytically and experimentally as a representative combinatorial problem. Their analysis identifies critical temperatures, indicating that temperature can mark important changes in system behavior. They suggest that understanding these temperatures could help improve neural-network performance. The contribution combines a faster approximate equilibrium calculation with analysis of how the resulting optimization dynamics behave.
neurips-1988-optimization-by-mean-field-.tldr: Mean field annealing replaces discrete stochastic variables with approximate averages, reaching fixed-temperature equilibrium substantially faster in the reported comparison.

paragraphs: This study evaluates neural networks that identify five commercial aircraft from radar backscatter measurements. It examines two network types: a multilayer perceptron and a frequency-sensitive competitive learning network. Their classification performance is compared with nearest-neighbor and maximum-likelihood methods, placing the neural approaches alongside established alternatives on the same problem.

The results indicate that the neural classifiers are relatively insensitive to changes in network topology and to noise levels in the training data. For this task, changing the network's arrangement or training-data noise does not strongly change performance. This is useful information about the behavior of the classifiers, separate from how accurately they classify aircraft overall.

The traditional methods outperform the simple neural classifiers studied. The authors nevertheless see potential for improved neural-network performance. The distinction matters: the observed result favors the traditional algorithms, while the case for better neural methods remains prospective. The paper therefore offers both a direct comparative finding and evidence about which changes the tested networks tolerate relatively well.
neurips-1988-performance-of-synthetic-ne.tldr: Traditional classifiers outperform the tested neural networks on aircraft radar identification, although the networks show relative insensitivity to topology and training noise.

paragraphs: The paper studies how neural networks generalize from examples by choosing a deliberately simple learning problem. It considers perceptrons learning linearly separable functions, focusing on the majority function: the output is one when more than half of the inputs are on. This creates a tractable setting for examining questions that arise in larger learning systems.

The motivating questions include how many examples and training cycles a task needs, how inputs should be represented, and which training examples are useful. The authors note that practical rules of thumb exist but rigorous results are scarce. Their case study seeks concrete numerical evidence and some analytical understanding within a problem simple enough to examine closely.

They find that many aspects of generalization seen in multilayer networks on large, difficult tasks also appear in this simpler domain. That makes the majority-function setting informative beyond its immediate task. The contribution is a manageable case study that reproduces broader learning phenomena and gives those phenomena a setting where more precise analysis is possible.
neurips-1988-scaling-and-generalization-.tldr: Perceptrons learning the majority function reproduce several generalization phenomena associated with larger networks while allowing more concrete analysis.

paragraphs: The paper offers a statistical interpretation of Kanerva's sparse distributed memory. Ordinarily, this model is understood as an associative memory that retrieves stored information. Near or beyond its capacity, that behavior breaks down. The authors argue that the computation in this regime can instead be understood as statistical prediction.

Mathematical results establish a broader framework in which the standard sparse distributed memory formulation becomes a special case. This changes how one interprets overloaded operation: failure to behave as an associative store does not by itself describe everything the system is computing. The statistical view supplies another account of its output and another objective against which it can be assessed.

The framework suggests ways to improve the model. One proposed procedure draws on genetic algorithms to increase predictive usefulness. Another aims to improve capacity when the model is used as an associative memory. These are presented as enhancements suggested by the new viewpoint, connecting a reinterpretation of existing behavior with possible changes to both prediction and storage.
neurips-1988-statistical-prediction-with.tldr: Sparse distributed memory can be interpreted as a statistical predictor near or beyond capacity, suggesting improvements to prediction and associative storage.

paragraphs: SYREN recognizes syllables by using changes in a speech signal over time. It classifies how quickly formant centers move and in which direction, then adaptively associates these transition events with syllables. The approach treats the movement of speech features as information for recognition, making temporal structure central to the classification task.

The system represents time in two ways. Delay lines make timing explicit by arranging delayed information spatially within the network. Other timing information is implicit in when units activate, how their activity decays, and the delays between transitions. The formant-classification subnetworks using these dynamics are described as analogous to visual motion detectors.

SYREN recognizes all of its training syllables and achieves 79 percent recognition on unseen data in a test involving six repetitions of 24 consonant-vowel syllables. The difference between training and unseen performance shows the distinction between fitting learned examples and recognizing new ones. The contribution combines explicit delays with internal activation dynamics to use speech transitions for syllable recognition.
neurips-1988-temporal-representations-in.tldr: SYREN combines delay lines and timed neural activity to recognize syllables from formant transitions, achieving 79 percent recognition on unseen data.

paragraphs: The paper presents compact integrated circuits that implement a winner-take-all function, selecting a winning response from competing inputs. The authors designed, fabricated, and tested a series of these circuits using CMOS technology. The contribution therefore includes physical circuit realization, taking the neural computation through implementation and testing.

The circuits are analog and operate continuously in time. Their central scaling property is that the amount of interconnect grows linearly with the number of inputs. This is the meaning of the O(n) claim: increasing the size of the competition requires proportionally more wiring. It describes interconnection complexity rather than establishing a corresponding bound on the time required to select a winner.

The authors also modify the winner-take-all circuit to compute local nonlinear inhibition. This extends the circuit approach from selecting a winner to a related form of local suppression. Together, the designs show how compact analog hardware can implement competitive neural operations while keeping interconnection requirements linear for the winner-take-all function.
neurips-1988-winner-take-all-networks-of.tldr: Fabricated analog CMOS circuits implement winner-take-all selection with linear interconnect complexity and can be adapted for local nonlinear inhibition.
